title: The exploitation of human suffering by the Hollywood machine

commenti.body:
Suffering is just as valid a topic for art as anything else - if you whitewash all media to be sunshine and rainbows, then it all starts to look fake and forced.

There is certainly such thing as works of art that offer nothing but exploitation of sympathy or sadness or such. I wouldn't say 12 Years a Slave is one of them, particularly. It's not an incredible work of art or anything imo, but it relates a real story that is fairly incredible, shines a light on a lesser-known aspect of a real historical evil, and reflects some of the struggles that persist to this day. 

It isn't all sadness and suffering, either - on the positive side it deals with how people maintain courage, dignity, and identity through such extreme limitation, exploitation, and suffering as is depicted. It deals with the compromises people are and aren't willing to make even when all choice appears to have been stripped from them, and how hope can persist through years of hopelessness.

Again, I didn't really find 12 Years a Slave to be a landmark important movie or anything. But it certainly does enough to justify itself being more than suffering-porn or whatnot, it isn't worthless besides depicting suffering.

I think it's a provocative perspective and I can see where you're coming from. The filming of sex is regularly described as exploitative (production conditions aside, pornography is said to "objectify" people), so why not depictions of suffering? 

The problem, for me, is where that logic then leads. Would you also ban other ways of representing suffering e.g. novels? Poems? Songs? 

And, if not, why not? 

Another way of putting it: is there something particular to cinema that lends itself to exploitation in a way that other media, such as novels, do not? I'm not sure there is. It seems to me that a good novel can be every bit as vivid in its representation of suffering than a movie, but I'll allow that they are very different. (Images are not the same as words, even if we often use the word 'imagery' to describe one of the effects of writing.)

I don't have the answers, but these are the sorts of questions your position would raise, I think...

I think your argument only works if you endorse the premise that the only purpose of film is to entertain.  Humoring this premise for a second, if entertainment is the sole purpose of a film, than of course any portrayal of suffering that gets at anything true or visceral is going to feel exploitative.  

However, I believe that film can exist outside the goal of pure entertainment to provide valuable experiences and information to audiences.  12 Years A Slave, for example, is a realistic, harrowing depiction of a historical atrocity through the eyes of the people who experienced it.  In portraying these horrors on-screen, 12 Years A Slave succeeds in inspiring empathy for the plight of enslaved people for an audience that would otherwise struggle to relate, provides historically accurate insight into the true brutality & extent of suffering that existed within the institution of slavery, and portrays a poignant story of human resilience that is emotionally impactful to audiences.  

I think it is important context to note that America in the present-day still struggles to acknowledge & properly educate about the horrors of slavery.  Where I grew up in the South, it was not uncommon for teachers to spin tall tales about "happy slaves," and even in the present, there have been many attempts by people to codify "positive" portrayals of slavery into our textbooks and educational curricula.  In a society like this, 12 Years A Slave acts an important counter to egregiously common falsehoods about the institution of slavery itself.

For that impact alone, I'd counter that the film is not exploitative but simply historically accurate.
